claim: RNA sequencing of anterior poles from uninjured animals identified 203 genes with significantly higher expression (padj <0.05) in pole-containing pieces compared to flanking pieces.
source: Differential gene expression analysis identified 203 genes with significantly higher (padj <0.05) expression in pole-containing pieces compared to flanking pieces from uninjured animals (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by RNA sequencing data and differential expression analysis performed by the authors.

claim: In the anterior blastema at 72 hours post amputation, 86 genes had pole-enriched expression (padj <0.05).
source: In the anterior blastema (an unpigmented outgrowth of differentiating tissue), 86 genes had pole-enriched expression (padj <0.05) (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing data from regenerating trunks at 72 hours post amputation.

claim: 51 genes had enriched expression in the poles of both uninjured and regenerating animals.
source: 51 genes had enriched expression in the poles of both uninjured and regenerating animals and these included the previously published anterior-pole genes foxD, notum, zic-1, and follistatin (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of RNA sequencing data from both uninjured and regenerating animals.

claim: Previously published anterior-pole genes foxD, notum, zic-1, and follistatin were among the genes with enriched expression in poles of both uninjured and regenerating animals.
source: 51 genes had enriched expression in the poles of both uninjured and regenerating animals and these included the previously published anterior-pole genes foxD, notum, zic-1, and follistatin (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1A, B).
evidence: The claim references previously published genes and confirms their expression in the current dataset.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing identified 198 genes with significantly higher expression (p<0.05) in posterior-pole cells compared to non-pole posterior muscle cells.
source: Using single-cell differential expression (SCDE) analysis (Kharchenko et al., 2014), we identified 198 genes with significantly higher expression (p<0.05) in posterior-pole cells compared to non-pole posterior muscle cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data and differential expression analysis.

claim: wnt1, pitx, and islet1 were in the top 16% of genes ranked by enrichment in posterior-pole cells.
source: wnt1, pitx, and islet1 were in the top 16% of those 198 genes ranked by enrichment in posterior-pole cells (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ranking analysis of the single-cell RNA sequencing data.

claim: 12 new genes expressed in the anterior pole were identified by whole-mount in situ hybridization.
source: We assessed the in vivo expression of 133 candidate anterior-pole genes and 96 candidate posterior pole genes by whole-mount in situ hybridization (WISH) and identified 12 new genes expressed in the anterior pole (Figure 1B) and 10 new genes expressed at the posterior pole (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization experiments validating RNA sequencing candidates.

claim: 10 new genes expressed at the posterior pole were identified by whole-mount in situ hybridization.
source: We assessed the in vivo expression of 133 candidate anterior-pole genes and 96 candidate posterior pole genes by whole-mount in situ hybridization (WISH) and identified 12 new genes expressed in the anterior pole (Figure 1B) and 10 new genes expressed at the posterior pole (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization experiments validating RNA sequencing candidates.

claim: New pole genes include those encoding a predicted secreted factor (kallmann1), cell-surface receptors (ror1, ephr4, ephr5, pcdh9, dcc, ddr2), and transcription factors (islet2, musculin, nr4A).
source: The new pole genes included those encoding a predicted secreted factor (kallmann1), cell-surface receptors (ror1, ephr4, ephr5, pcdh9, dcc, ddr2), and transcription factors (islet2, musculin, nr4A) (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by identification and classification of genes based on their predicted protein products.

claim: Some genes such as kallmann1, ephr5, and dd_20026 were expressed in both anterior and posterior poles.
source: Interestingly, some of these genes, such as kallmann1, ephr5, and dd_20026 were expressed in both anterior and posterior poles, identifying molecular similarity between these structures (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 1A-C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing expression in both poles.

claim: Expression of genes in both anterior and posterior poles identifies molecular similarity between these structures.
source: Interestingly, some of these genes, such as kallmann1, ephr5, and dd_20026 were expressed in both anterior and posterior poles, identifying molecular similarity between these structures (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 1A-C).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the expression data showing shared gene expression between poles.

claim: nr4A encodes the S. mediterranea homolog to proteins of the NR4A nuclear receptor family.
source: nr4A encodes the S. mediterranea homolog to proteins of the NR4A nuclear receptor family, which are found broadly in metazoans (Bridgham et al., 2010; Escriva et al., 2004) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis and comparison to known NR4A family members.

claim: NR4A nuclear receptor family proteins are found broadly in metazoans.
source: nr4A encodes the S. mediterranea homolog to proteins of the NR4A nuclear receptor family, which are found broadly in metazoans (Bridgham et al., 2010; Escriva et al., 2004) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature on NR4A family distribution.

claim: RNAi of nr4A resulted in the progressive formation of posterior ectopic eyes in uninjured animals.
source: RNAi of nr4A resulted in the progressive formation of posterior ectopic eyes in uninjured animals (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging of animals subjected to nr4A RNAi over time.

claim: After initiation of nr4A RNAi, the distance between the original eyes and the head tip progressively decreased.
source: After initiation of nr4A RNAi, the distance between the original eyes and the head tip progressively decreased.
evidence: The claim is supported by observations and measurements from live imaging over the RNAi time course.

claim: By 6 weeks of nr4A RNAi, an additional eye pair emerged just posterior to the original eyes.
source: By 6 weeks of nr4A RNAi, an additional eye pair emerged just posterior to the original eyes.
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging observations at specific time points during RNAi.

claim: As time progressed during nr4A RNAi, the original and second eye pairs became closer to the head tip and decreased in size.
source: As time progressed, the original and second eye pairs became closer to the head tip and decreased in size.
evidence: The claim is supported by longitudinal observations of individual animals during nr4A RNAi.

claim: A third eye pair posterior to the second eye pair appeared during nr4A RNAi, resulting in animals with six eyes.
source: A third eye pair, posterior to the second eye pair then appeared, resulting in animals with six eyes.
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging showing iterative eye formation.

claim: With ongoing nr4A inhibition, animals developed as many as 10 eyes after 16 weeks of RNAi.
source: This iterative process continued with ongoing nr4A inhibition, generating animals with as many as 10 eyes after 16 weeks of RNAi.
evidence: The claim is supported by long-term observations of nr4A RNAi animals.

claim: By 12 weeks of nr4A RNAi, uninjured animals developed dorsal outgrowths at their tail tips.
source: By 12 weeks of nr4A RNAi, uninjured animals developed dorsal outgrowths at their tail tips, suggesting that nr4A influences both head and tail tip pattern (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging of tail phenotypes during nr4A RNAi.

claim: nr4A influences both head and tail tip pattern.
source: By 12 weeks of nr4A RNAi, uninjured animals developed dorsal outgrowths at their tail tips, suggesting that nr4A influences both head and tail tip pattern (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on phenotypes observed at both ends of the animal.

claim: After transverse amputation, nr4A(RNAi) trunk fragments were capable of regenerating heads with normal eye number.
source: After transverse amputation of heads and tails, nr4A(RNAi) trunk fragments were capable of regenerating heads with normal eye number and tails without outgrowths (Figure 2A,B), indicating that the nr4A phenotype is most readily apparent during tissue turnover associated with maintenance of anatomical pattern.
evidence: The claim is supported by regeneration experiments following amputation of nr4A RNAi animals.

claim: After transverse amputation, nr4A(RNAi) trunk fragments were capable of regenerating tails without outgrowths.
source: After transverse amputation of heads and tails, nr4A(RNAi) trunk fragments were capable of regenerating heads with normal eye number and tails without outgrowths (Figure 2A,B), indicating that the nr4A phenotype is most readily apparent during tissue turnover associated with maintenance of anatomical pattern.
evidence: The claim is supported by regeneration experiments following amputation of nr4A RNAi animals.

claim: The nr4A phenotype is most readily apparent during tissue turnover associated with maintenance of anatomical pattern.
source: After transverse amputation of heads and tails, nr4A(RNAi) trunk fragments were capable of regenerating heads with normal eye number and tails without outgrowths (Figure 2A,B), indicating that the nr4A phenotype is most readily apparent during tissue turnover associated with maintenance of anatomical pattern.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the difference between homeostatic and regenerative phenotypes.

claim: The heads of nr4A(RNAi) animals at 9 weeks developed ectopic eyes labeled by opsin expression.
source: In addition to ectopic eyes, labeled by an RNA probe to opsin, the heads of nr4A(RNAi) animals developed internal (along the AP axis) ectopic foci of epidermal cells normally restricted to the animal periphery at the dorsal-ventral (DV)-median plane (laminB+ and NB.22.1e+ cells) (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence in situ hybridization with opsin probe.

claim: The heads of nr4A(RNAi) animals developed internal ectopic foci of epidermal cells (laminB+ and NB.22.1e+ cells) normally restricted to the animal periphery at the dorsal-ventral median plane.
source: In addition to ectopic eyes, labeled by an RNA probe to opsin, the heads of nr4A(RNAi) animals developed internal (along the AP axis) ectopic foci of epidermal cells normally restricted to the animal periphery at the dorsal-ventral (DV)-median plane (laminB+ and NB.22.1e+ cells) (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH showing ectopic expression of epidermal markers.

claim: Marginal adhesive gland cells (mag-1+) are normally present in a prepharyngeal domain posterior to the eyes and along the body margin posteriorly from this zone.
source: Marginal adhesive gland cells (mag-1+) are normally present in a prepharyngeal domain posterior to the eyes and along the body margin posteriorly from this zone (Zayas et al., 2010) (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim describes normal expression pattern and is supported by citation and current data.

claim: The distance from the original eyes to the posterior end of the mag-1+ domain was significantly greater in nr4A(RNAi) animals than in control animals.
source: The distance from the original eyes to the posterior end of the mag-1+ domain was significantly greater in nr4A(RNAi) animals than in control animals (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of mag-1 expression domains.

claim: FISH with neural markers ChAT and dd_3524 showed a loss of the head region between the apex of the head and the anterior aspect of the brain following nr4A RNAi.
source: FISH with neural markers ChAT and dd_3524, which are expressed in the inverted 'U'-shaped cephalic ganglia, showed a loss of the head region between the apex of the head and the anterior aspect of the brain following nr4A RNAi (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH showing altered neural marker expression patterns.

claim: Ectopic foci of DV boundary epidermal cells (laminB+ and NB.22.1e+) appeared internally in the tails of nr4A(RNAi) animals.
source: Similar to the changes we observed in the head, ectopic foci of DV boundary epidermal cells (laminB+ and NB.22.1e+) appeared internally (along the AP axis) in the tails of nr4A(RNAi) animals (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH showing ectopic epidermal marker expression in tails.

claim: The secretory mag-1+ cells normally restricted to the body margin around the tail periphery appeared internally along the midline of tails following nr4A RNAi.
source: The secretory mag-1+ cells normally restricted to the body margin around the tail periphery also appeared internally along the midline of tails following nr4A RNAi (Figure 2D), resulting in aberrant tail-tip patterning.
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH showing ectopic mag-1 expression in tails.

claim: The mislocalization of differentiated tissues in nr4A(RNAi) animals demonstrates that nr4A activity is required for normal restriction of tissues to their proper domains at both extreme ends of the AP axis.
source: The mislocalization of differentiated tissues in nr4A(RNAi) animals demonstrates that nr4A activity is required for normal restriction of tissues to their proper domains at both extreme ends of the AP axis.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the observed tissue mislocalization phenotypes.

claim: In uninjured nr4A(RNAi) animals at 9 weeks of RNAi, expression domains of ndl-4, sFRP-1, notum, and foxD were retracted from the head tip and expanded posteriorly.
source: In uninjured nr4A(RNAi) animals analyzed at 9 weeks of RNAi, these expression domains were retracted from the head tip and expanded posteriorly (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH and quantification of PCG expression domains.

claim: foxD+; notum+ anterior pole cells were no longer present in a cluster at the head tip in nr4A(RNAi) animals, but instead were found scattered between the eyes.
source: foxD+; notum+ anterior pole cells were no longer present in a cluster at the head tip, but instead were found scattered between the eyes (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH showing altered anterior pole cell distribution.

claim: Amputated nr4A(RNAi) animals were able to regenerate anterior poles by 72 hours post amputation.
source: Amputated nr4A(RNAi) animals were able to regenerate anterior poles by 72hpa (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH showing anterior pole marker expression in regenerating blastemas.

claim: At 7 days post amputation in nr4A(RNAi) animals, the anterior-pole-cell cluster was absent from the head tip and instead was disorganized and shifted posteriorly.
source: However, at 7 days post amputation (7dpa) the anterior-pole-cell cluster was absent from the head tip and instead was disorganized and shifted posteriorly (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH showing anterior pole cell distribution in regenerated heads.

claim: At 9 weeks post-initiation of nr4A RNAi, the posterior-most expression domain of wnt1 was absent, leaving a gap between the tip of the tail and wnt1 expression.
source: At 9 weeks post-initiation of nr4A RNAi, the posterior-most expression domain of wnt1 was absent, leaving a gap between the tip of the tail and wnt1 expression (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH showing altered wnt1 expression in tails.

claim: The localized expression of wnt11-2 at the tail tip was abrogated by nr4A RNAi.
source: Furthermore, the localized expression of wnt11-2 at the tail tip was also abrogated by nr4A RNAi (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH showing loss of wnt11-2 expression at the tail tip.

claim: An increase in the area of wnt11-1 expression was observed in the tails of nr4A(RNAi) animals.
source: We also observed an increase in the area of wnt11-1 expression in the tails of nr4A(RNAi) animals (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH and quantification of wnt11-1 expression domain area.

claim: In the midbody region, nr4A RNAi did not significantly affect the location of the posterior boundaries of the expression domains of ndl-2, ndl-3, ndl-5, and wnt2.
source: Specifically, the location of the posterior boundaries of the expression domains of ndl-2, ndl-3, ndl-5, and wnt2 were normal compared to the control (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, Supplementary file 1D), despite the anterior boundaries of their expression domains being shifted (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of PCG expression domain boundaries.

claim: The length of ptk7 expression domain in the midbody was not significantly altered by nr4A RNAi.
source: Additionally, the length of ptk7 expression domain, defined by the distance between its anterior and posterior boundaries in the midbody, was not significantly altered by nr4A RNAi (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of ptk7 expression domain length.

claim: The dorsal-specific expression of bmp4 was largely intact in nr4A(RNAi) animals, with an increase in its expression in the esophagus compared with control animals.
source: The dorsal-specific expression of bmp4 was largely intact in nr4A(RNAi) animals, with an increase in its expression in the esophagus compared with its expression in control animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization showing bmp4 expression pattern.

claim: There was no ectopic ventral bmp4 expression in nr4A(RNAi) animals.
source: There was no ectopic ventral bmp4 expression in nr4A(RNAi) animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization showing normal dorsal restriction of bmp4.

claim: The midline expression domains of slit and ephR1 were broadened medial-laterally and were disorganized in the head of nr4A(RNAi) animals.
source: The midline expression domains of slit and ephR1 were broadened medial-laterally and were disorganized in the head of nr4A(RNAi) animals (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH showing altered midline marker expression in heads.

claim: slit expression was reduced in the tail of nr4A(RNAi) animals, but its midline expression in the rest of the body was comparable to that of control animals.
source: slit expression was also reduced in the tail of nr4A(RNAi) animals, but its midline expression in the rest of the body was comparable to that of control animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH showing region-specific changes in slit expression.

claim: nr4A inhibition does not cause a gross midline-patterning defect, but rather disrupts slit expression specifically in the head and tail.
source: This suggests nr4A inhibition does not cause a gross midline-patterning defect, but rather disrupts slit expression specifically in the head and tail, likely associated with disruption in the pattern of anterior and posterior poles, which play important roles in midline specification and patterning (Hayashi et al., 2011; Currie and Pearson, 2013; März et al., 2013; Scimone et al., 2014; Vásquez-Doorman and Petersen, 2014; Vogg et al., 2014; Oderberg et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the slit expression data combined with knowledge from cited literature.

claim: nr4A inhibition causes anterior PCGs to shift posteriorly and posterior PCGs to shift anteriorly.
source: Taken together, our PCG expression analysis showed that nr4A inhibition causes anterior PCGs to shift posteriorly and posterior PCGs to shift anteriorly (Figure 3D) while largely sparing midbody, midline, and DV PCG expression domains outside of the head and tail ends.
evidence: The claim summarizes the overall pattern of PCG expression changes observed.

claim: nr4A inhibition largely spares midbody, midline, and DV PCG expression domains outside of the head and tail ends.
source: Taken together, our PCG expression analysis showed that nr4A inhibition causes anterior PCGs to shift posteriorly and posterior PCGs to shift anteriorly (Figure 3D) while largely sparing midbody, midline, and DV PCG expression domains outside of the head and tail ends.
evidence: The claim summarizes the regional specificity of PCG expression changes.

claim: nr4A was predominantly expressed in planarian muscle in both intact animals and regenerating blastemas.
source: Consistent with its role in patterning, nr4A was predominantly expressed in planarian muscle in both intact animals and regenerating blastemas (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH showing co-expression of nr4A with muscle marker collagen.

claim: A higher proportion of muscle cells expressed nr4A in the head and tail than in the pre-pharyngeal region.
source: A higher proportion of muscle cells expressed nr4A in the head and tail than in the pre-pharyngeal region (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of nr4A expression in muscle cells across different body regions.

claim: nr4A expression was enriched at the ends of the AP axis, including in the posterior pole.
source: Although its expression was enriched at the ends of the AP axis, including in the posterior pole (Figure 4C), nr4A was also expressed broadly in body-wall muscle (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH showing nr4A expression pattern along the AP axis.

claim: nr4A was also expressed broadly in body-wall muscle.
source: Although its expression was enriched at the ends of the AP axis, including in the posterior pole (Figure 4C), nr4A was also expressed broadly in body-wall muscle (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH showing widespread nr4A expression in muscle.

claim: Mapping nr4A expression onto single-cell expression data showed that nr4A was most highly expressed in muscle cells, with some expression in neoblasts.
source: Mapping nr4A expression onto single-cell expression data (Wurtzel et al., 2015) showed that nr4A was most highly expressed in muscle cells, with some expression in neoblasts (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of nr4A expression in published single-cell RNA sequencing data.

claim: nr4A was expressed in longitudinal, circular, and DV muscle fiber types, but not in intestinal muscle cells.
source: By using a single-cell sequencing dataset of different muscle cell subtypes (Scimone et al., 2018), we found that nr4A was expressed in longitudinal, circular, and DV muscle fiber types, but not in intestinal muscle cells (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of nr4A expression in published muscle subtype single-cell data.

claim: During regeneration, nr4A expression was upregulated by 48 hours post amputation and increased in level at 72 hours post amputation at both anterior- and posterior-facing wound sites.
source: During regeneration, nr4A expression was upregulated by 48 hpa and increased in level at 72 hpa at both anterior- and posterior-facing wound sites (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization showing nr4A expression during regeneration time course.

claim: nr4A expression time-course behavior in regeneration was similar to that of many anterior and posterior PCGs.
source: This expression time-course behavior in regeneration was similar to that of many anterior and posterior PCGs (Wenemoser et al., 2012; Wurtzel et al., 2015) (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to published PCG expression dynamics during regeneration.

claim: Unlike canonical muscle-expressed patterning factors, nr4A was upregulated at both anterior- and posterior-facing wounds.
source: However, unlike canonical muscle-expressed pattering factors, nr4A was upregulated at both anterior- and posterior-facing wounds – having both anterior- and posterior-PCG-like expression dynamics during regeneration (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of nr4A expression dynamics to other PCGs during regeneration.

claim: RNA sequencing identified 56 genes with significant expression changes in the head (padj <0.05) in at least one time point in nr4A(RNAi) animals compared to controls.
source: We identified 56 and 41 genes with significant expression changes in the head and tail (padj <0.05), respectively, in at least one time point in nr4A(RNAi) animals compared to controls (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing and differential expression analysis.

claim: RNA sequencing identified 41 genes with significant expression changes in the tail (padj <0.05) in at least one time point in nr4A(RNAi) animals compared to controls.
source: We identified 56 and 41 genes with significant expression changes in the head and tail (padj <0.05), respectively, in at least one time point in nr4A(RNAi) animals compared to controls (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing and differential expression analysis.

claim: The majority of genes with significant expression changes (49/56 in the head and 36/41 in the tail) were downregulated in nr4A(RNAi) animals.
source: The majority of these genes (49/56 in the head and 36/41 in the tail) were downregulated and most (32/56 in the head and 19/41 in the tail) were genes known to have muscle-enriched expression from available single-cell RNA sequencing data on wild-type animals (Wurtzel et al., 2015) (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of the direction of expression changes in RNA sequencing data.

claim: Most genes with significant expression changes (32/56 in the head and 19/41 in the tail) were genes known to have muscle-enriched expression.
source: The majority of these genes (49/56 in the head and 36/41 in the tail) were downregulated and most (32/56 in the head and 19/41 in the tail) were genes known to have muscle-enriched expression from available single-cell RNA sequencing data on wild-type animals (Wurtzel et al., 2015) (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to published single-cell expression data.

claim: 16 genes were significantly affected by nr4A in both the head and the tail.
source: 16 genes were significantly affected by nr4A in both the head and the tail.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of differentially expressed genes between head and tail datasets.

claim: A high proportion (11/16) of genes affected by nr4A in both head and tail were genes known to be expressed in muscle.
source: A high proportion (11/16) of those (e.g., dd_9565 (col21a1) and dd_11601 (qki)) were genes known to be expressed in muscle (Wurtzel et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to published muscle expression data.

claim: nr4A RNAi reduced the body-wide expression of some genes (e.g., dd_9565 (col21a1), dd_1706 (psapl1)).
source: Whereas nr4A RNAi reduced the body-wide expression of some genes (e.g., dd_9565 (col21a1), dd_1706 (psapl1)), it inhibited the expression of other genes more specifically in the head and tail (e.g., dd_2972, dd_11683 (ca12), dd_950 (vim)) (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH showing expression patterns of nr4A-regulated genes.

claim: nr4A RNAi inhibited the expression of other genes more specifically in the head and tail (e.g., dd_2972, dd_11683 (ca12), dd_950 (vim)).
source: Whereas nr4A RNAi reduced the body-wide expression of some genes (e.g., dd_9565 (col21a1), dd_1706 (psapl1)), it inhibited the expression of other genes more specifically in the head and tail (e.g., dd_2972, dd_11683 (ca12), dd_950 (vim)) (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH showing region-specific expression changes.

claim: One-third of the nr4A-regulated genes were enriched in their expression in the head and the tail compared to midbody regions.
source: One-third of the nr4A-regulated genes, including 9 of 16 genes affected by nr4A in both the head and the tail, were enriched in their expression in the head and the tail compared to midbody regions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of gene expression patterns across body regions using published data.

claim: Following initiation of RNAi, ndl-2 was downregulated in the head by week 3.
source: Following initiation of RNAi, ndl-2 and ndl-5 were downregulated in the head (by week 3 and 4, respectively), wnt11-1 was upregulated in the tail (by week 2), and nlg-8 was downregulated in the tail (by week 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing time course data.

claim: Following initiation of RNAi, ndl-5 was downregulated in the head by week 4.
source: Following initiation of RNAi, ndl-2 and ndl-5 were downregulated in the head (by week 3 and 4, respectively), wnt11-1 was upregulated in the tail (by week 2), and nlg-8 was downregulated in the tail (by week 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing time course data.

claim: Following initiation of RNAi, wnt11-1 was upregulated in the tail by week 2.
source: Following initiation of RNAi, ndl-2 and ndl-5 were downregulated in the head (by week 3 and 4, respectively), wnt11-1 was upregulated in the tail (by week 2), and nlg-8 was downregulated in the tail (by week 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing time course data.

claim: Following initiation of RNAi, nlg-8 was downregulated in the tail by week 3.
source: Following initiation of RNAi, ndl-2 and ndl-5 were downregulated in the head (by week 3 and 4, respectively), wnt11-1 was upregulated in the tail (by week 2), and nlg-8 was downregulated in the tail (by week 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing time course data.

claim: ndl-2, ndl-5, wnt11-1, and nlg-8 encode FGFRL, Wnt, and Bmp-regulatory proteins and have been implicated in patterning.
source: These genes encode FGFRL (ndl-2,–5), Wnt (wnt11-1), and Bmp-regulatory (nlg-8) proteins and have been implicated in patterning (Molina et al., 2007; Gurley et al., 2010; Lander and Petersen, 2016; Scimone et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature on these genes.

claim: nr4A is required for the expression of numerous muscle-expressed genes at the planarian head and tail ends, including those encoding extracellular matrix proteins and PCGs.
source: These data show that nr4A is required for the expression of numerous muscle-expressed genes at the planarian head and tail ends, including those encoding extracellular matrix proteins and PCGs.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the RNA sequencing and FISH data.

claim: By 9 weeks of RNAi, uninjured nr4A(RNAi) animals showed loss of longitudinal, circular, and diagonal muscle fibers in the head compared to control animals.
source: By 9 weeks of RNAi, when multiple ectopic eyes were present, uninjured nr4A(RNAi) animals showed loss of longitudinal, circular, and diagonal muscle fibers and a decreased number of collagen+ muscle cells in the head compared to control animals (Figure 6A–C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence with muscle antibody and quantification.

claim: By 9 weeks of RNAi, uninjured nr4A(RNAi) animals showed a decreased number of collagen+ muscle cells in the head compared to control animals.
source: By 9 weeks of RNAi, when multiple ectopic eyes were present, uninjured nr4A(RNAi) animals showed loss of longitudinal, circular, and diagonal muscle fibers and a decreased number of collagen+ muscle cells in the head compared to control animals (Figure 6A–C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH with collagen probe and cell counting.

claim: Muscle fibers were not significantly affected in the trunk or tail of nr4A(RNAi) animals at 9 weeks of RNAi.
source: By contrast, muscle fibers were not significantly affected in the trunk or tail of nr4A(RNAi) animals and collagen+ muscle cell numbers were normal in nr4A(RNAi) animal tails (Figure 6A–C Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification showing no significant changes.

claim: collagen+ muscle cell numbers were normal in nr4A(RNAi) animal tails at 9 weeks of RNAi.
source: By contrast, muscle fibers were not significantly affected in the trunk or tail of nr4A(RNAi) animals and collagen+ muscle cell numbers were normal in nr4A(RNAi) animal tails (Figure 6A–C Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH and cell counting showing no significant changes.

claim: At 4 weeks of RNAi, nr4A(RNAi) animals showed no changes in muscle fibers or collagen+ cell numbers in the head or tail compared to control animals.
source: Similar analyses of nr4A(RNAi) animals at an earlier time point (4 weeks of RNAi) showed no changes in muscle fibers or collagen+ cell numbers in the head or tail compared to control animals (Figure 6A,C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and cell counting at an earlier time point.

claim: The numbers of new muscle cells (EdU+; collagen+) in the head tip of nr4A(RNAi) animals at 9 weeks were significantly decreased compared to similar regions in control animals.
source: The numbers of new muscle cells (EdU+; collagen+) in the head tip of nr4A(RNAi) animals, but not in the posterior head, trunk, or tail, were significantly decreased compared to similar regions (by location and area) in control animals (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU labeling and quantification of new muscle cells.

claim: The numbers of new muscle cells in the posterior head, trunk, or tail of nr4A(RNAi) animals at 9 weeks were not significantly different from control animals.
source: The numbers of new muscle cells (EdU+; collagen+) in the head tip of nr4A(RNAi) animals, but not in the posterior head, trunk, or tail, were significantly decreased compared to similar regions (by location and area) in control animals (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU labeling and quantification showing no significant changes in these regions.

claim: There were no significant differences in the total amount of EdU incorporation (all EdU+ cells) in head tip, posterior head, trunk, or tail regions between nr4A(RNAi) and control animals at 9 weeks.
source: By contrast, there were no significant differences in the total amount of EdU incorporation (all EdU+ cells) in those regions between nr4A(RNAi) and control animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU labeling and quantification of all EdU+ cells.

claim: The numbers of new muscle cells anterior to the original eyes in nr4A(RNAi) animals were similar to the numbers anterior to the newest eyes in nr4A(RNAi) animals.
source: By contrast, the numbers of new muscle cells anterior to the eyes of controls and anterior to the newest eyes in nr4A(RNAi) animals were similar (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU labeling and quantification in different regions of nr4A RNAi animals.

claim: nr4A(RNAi) and control animals had comparable numbers of apoptotic cells in similar head tip regions as assessed by TUNEL.
source: nr4A(RNAi) and control animals had comparable numbers of apoptotic cells in similar head tip regions (by location and area) as assessed by TUNEL (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E), suggesting defective progenitor migratory targeting as opposed to increased cell death underlies muscle loss at the head tip.
evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL assay and quantification of apoptotic cells.

claim: Defective progenitor migratory targeting as opposed to increased cell death underlies muscle loss at the head tip in nr4A(RNAi) animals.
source: nr4A(RNAi) and control animals had comparable numbers of apoptotic cells in similar head tip regions (by location and area) as assessed by TUNEL (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E), suggesting defective progenitor migratory targeting as opposed to increased cell death underlies muscle loss at the head tip.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the TUNEL data showing no increase in apoptosis.

claim: nr4A was not required in general for muscle progenitor production and differentiation throughout the body.
source: These findings indicate that nr4A was not required in general for muscle progenitor production and differentiation throughout the body.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the region-specific nature of the muscle phenotype.

claim: The head-tip-specific muscle progenitor incorporation defect occurred after PCG and other gene expression changes were detected in the nr4A(RNAi) RNA sequencing data.
source: The head-tip-specific muscle progenitor incorporation defect occurred after PCG and other gene expression changes were detected in the nr4A(RNAi) RNA sequencing data.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of timing of gene expression changes and muscle phenotypes.

claim: Loss of muscle cells per se is not the cause of the PCG expression changes that occurred at earlier timepoints in the nr4A RNAi.
source: Together with the observation that muscle fiber loss was also head-restricted and a late-stage phenotype (absent at 4 weeks of RNAi), these findings suggest loss of muscle cells per se is not the cause of the PCG expression changes that occurred at earlier timepoints in the nr4A RNAi.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the temporal sequence of phenotypes.

claim: In the head, ndl-2 and ndl-5 expression domains shifted posteriorly relative to the eyes by 3 weeks of nr4A RNAi compared to control RNAi.
source: Specifically, in the head, ndl-2 and ndl-5 expression domains shifted posteriorly relative to the eyes by 3 weeks of nr4A RNAi compared to control RNAi (Figure 7A,B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B, Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH and quantification of PCG expression domains at 3 weeks.

claim: At 3 weeks of nr4A RNAi, the numbers of muscle cells and the appearance of muscle fibers were normal in the heads of nr4A(RNAi) animals.
source: At this time point, the numbers of muscle cells and the appearance of muscle fibers were normal in the heads of nr4A(RNAi) animals (Figure 6A,C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and cell counting at 3 weeks showing no changes.

claim: Mis-positioned anterior pole cells were the earliest abnormalities detected, becoming scattered between the eyes by two weeks after initiation of RNAi.
source: Mis-positioned anterior pole cells were the earliest abnormalities detected, becoming scattered between the eyes by two weeks after initiation of RNAi (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH showing anterior pole cell distribution at 2 weeks.

claim: The posterior shift of notum expression preceded detected changes in the expression of other head PCGs (ndl-2, ndl-4, ndl-5, sFRP-1).
source: This posterior shift of notum expression preceded detected changes in the expression of other head PCGs (ndl-2, ndl-4, ndl-5, sFRP-1), as well as changes in the distribution of marginal adhesive gland cells (Figure 7A,B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B, Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of timing of expression changes across multiple genes.

claim: The posterior shift of notum expression preceded changes in the distribution of marginal adhesive gland cells.
source: This posterior shift of notum expression preceded detected changes in the expression of other head PCGs (ndl-2, ndl-4, ndl-5, sFRP-1), as well as changes in the distribution of marginal adhesive gland cells (Figure 7A,B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B, Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of timing of pole cell and differentiated tissue changes.

claim: There were no apparent differences in head tip muscle fibers between control and nr4A(RNAi) animals after two weeks of RNAi when pole cells were already gone from this location.
source: Consistent with our findings that muscle fiber loss at the head tip occurs at late stages of the phenotype (after 4 weeks - Figure 6A,B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B), we observed no apparent differences in head tip muscle fibers between control and nr4A(RNAi) animals after two weeks of RNAi when pole cells were already gone from this location (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence showing normal muscle at 2 weeks despite pole cell changes.

claim: In the tail, the posterior pole shifted anteriorly by three weeks after initiation of RNAi.
source: In the tail, the posterior pole shifted anteriorly by three weeks after initiation of RNAi (Figure 7D, Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH showing wnt1 expression changes at 3 weeks.

claim: The clustered expression of wnt11-2 at the tail tip decreased by three weeks after initiation of RNAi.
source: The clustered expression of wnt11-2 at the tail tip also decreased by this time point (Figure 7D, Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH showing wnt11-2 expression changes at 3 weeks.

claim: No changes in mag-1+ cells were apparent at three weeks after initiation of RNAi.
source: However, no changes in mag-1+ cells were apparent at this time (Figure 7D, Supplementary file 1D), indicating that similar to the case of the anterior head tip, PCG pattern changes precede differentiated tissue shifts at the posterior extremity of nr4A(RNAi) animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH showing normal mag-1 expression at 3 weeks.

claim: PCG pattern changes precede differentiated tissue shifts at the posterior extremity of nr4A(RNAi) animals.
source: However, no changes in mag-1+ cells were apparent at this time (Figure 7D, Supplementary file 1D), indicating that similar to the case of the anterior head tip, PCG pattern changes precede differentiated tissue shifts at the posterior extremity of nr4A(RNAi) animals.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the temporal sequence of PCG and differentiated tissue changes.

claim: After just one week of nr4A RNAi, there was a quantifiable increase in the distance between notum+ cells and the head apex.
source: Even after just one week of nr4A RNAi, we observed a quantifiable increase in the distance between notum+ cells and the head apex (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, non-irradiated).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH and quantification at 1 week of RNAi.

claim: Irradiation suppressed the earliest detectable posterior shift of notum+ cells in nr4A(RNAi) animals.
source: Irradiation suppressed this earliest detectable posterior shift of notum+ cells in nr4A(RNAi) animals, demonstrating that anterior-pole changes were neoblast-dependent (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A irradiated).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH showing no pole cell shift in irradiated nr4A RNAi animals.

claim: Anterior-pole changes in nr4A(RNAi) animals were neoblast-dependent.
source: Irradiation suppressed this earliest detectable posterior shift of notum+ cells in nr4A(RNAi) animals, demonstrating that anterior-pole changes were neoblast-dependent (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A irradiated).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the irradiation experiment results.

claim: SMEDWI-1+ ectopic anterior pole cells were present at both early (2 weeks) and late (9 weeks) nr4A RNAi time points.
source: SMEDWI-1+ ectopic anterior pole cells were present at both early (2 weeks) and late (9 weeks) nr4A RNAi time points (Figure 8B), further indicating that new anterior pole cells are continually being targeted to ectopically posterior regions in nr4A(RNAi) animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH showing SMEDWI-1+ pole cells at multiple time points.

claim: New anterior pole cells are continually being targeted to ectopically posterior regions in nr4A(RNAi) animals.
source: SMEDWI-1+ ectopic anterior pole cells were present at both early (2 weeks) and late (9 weeks) nr4A RNAi time points (Figure 8B), further indicating that new anterior pole cells are continually being targeted to ectopically posterior regions in nr4A(RNAi) animals.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the presence of newly differentiated pole cells at ectopic locations.

claim: A greater proportion of foxD; nr4A(RNAi) animals lacked ectopic eyes than did control; nr4A(RNAi) animals.
source: A greater proportion of foxD; nr4A(RNAi) animals lacked ectopic eyes than did control; nr4A(RNAi) animals (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by phenotype scoring of double RNAi animals.

claim: The result that foxD; nr4A(RNAi) animals had fewer ectopic eyes was consistently observed in intact and pole-cut animal groups, and in biological replicates.
source: This result was consistently observed in intact and pole-cut animal groups, and in biological replicates (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple independent experiments showing the same result.

claim: qPCR showed similar levels of nr4A expression inhibition between foxD; nr4A(RNAi) and control; nr4A(RNAi) groups.
source: qPCR of animals at the end of the double RNAi period showed similar levels of nr4A expression inhibition between foxD; nr4A(RNAi) and control; nr4A(RNAi) groups (Figure 8D, Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR measurements of nr4A expression levels.

claim: The head patterning defects of nr4A RNAi are mediated, at least in part, by the mis-positioning of anterior pole cells.
source: Taken together with the fact that a posterior shift in anterior pole cells was the earliest observed change in nr4A(RNAi) animals, these results indicate that the head patterning defects of nr4A RNAi are mediated, at least in part, by the mis-positioning of anterior pole cells.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the double RNAi experiments and temporal analysis.

claim: The original eyes (and even older ectopic eyes) eventually faded and disappeared at the head tip as the nr4A(RNAi) phenotype progressed.
source: Tracking the fates of the eyes in individual animals after extended periods of continuous nr4A inhibition (as long as 21 weeks) showed that the original eyes (and even older ectopic eyes) eventually faded and disappeared at the head tip as the phenotype progressed (Figure 9A, Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by longitudinal tracking of individual animals over extended time periods.

claim: Eye progenitors iteratively shifted their targeting to the most posterior set of eyes, leaving the anterior eyes to decay.
source: As this process unfolded, eye progenitors iteratively shifted their targeting to the most posterior set of eyes, leaving the anterior eyes to decay.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the eye disappearance and new eye formation patterns.

claim: There were significantly more new eye cells (opsin+; SMEDWI+) in the newest (posterior) ectopic eyes than in older (more anterior) ectopic eyes.
source: Specifically, there were significantly more new eye cells (opsin+; SMEDWI+) in the newest (posterior) ectopic eyes than in older (more anterior) ectopic eyes (Figure 9B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of new eye cells in different eye pairs.

claim: The numbers of new eye cells produced in a given unit of time were similar between the eyes of control animals and the newest, posterior ectopic eyes in nr4A(RNAi) animals.
source: The numbers of new eye cells produced in a given unit of time were similar between the eyes of control animals and the newest, posterior ectopic eyes in nr4A(RNAi) animals (Figure 9B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification showing no significant difference in progenitor incorporation.

claim: Eye progenitor targeting continued to shift posteriorly after nr4A inhibition, iteratively producing ectopic eyes without reaching a stable tissue-pattern state.
source: These findings suggest that eye progenitor targeting continued to shift posteriorly after nr4A inhibition, iteratively producing ectopic eyes without reaching a stable tissue-pattern state.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the progenitor incorporation and eye fate tracking data.

claim: Planarian muscle cells express signaling molecules to promote positional identity.
source: In planarians, muscle cells express signaling molecules to promote positional identity.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: At the ends of the anterior-posterior axis, positional identity is determined by anterior and posterior poles, which are putative organizers.
source: At the ends of the anterior-posterior (AP) axis, positional identity is determined by anterior and posterior poles, which are putative organizers.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: NR4A is a transcription factor that helps regulate tissue pattern at both ends of the AP body axis.
source: We conclude NR4A is a transcription factor that helps regulate tissue pattern at both ends of the AP body axis.
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion of the study based on all presented data.

claim: The nr4A phenotype represents a patterning abnormality in which a stable anatomical pattern is not reached and instead iterative duplication of tissues continues to occur.
source: The nr4A phenotype represents a patterning abnormality in which a stable anatomical pattern is not reached and instead iterative duplication of tissues continues to occur.
evidence: The claim is a characterization of the unique nature of the nr4A phenotype.

claim: nr4A promotes pattern at planarian AP axis ends through restriction of patterning gene expression domains.
source: We propose that nr4A promotes pattern at planarian AP axis ends through restriction of patterning gene expression domains.
evidence: The claim is a proposed mechanism based on the observed PCG expression changes.
